tools.keywords: box shadow css generator shadow blur spread rgba inset
tools.title_tag: CSS Box Shadow Generator – Live Preview
tools.meta: Set offset, blur, spread, colour and opacity to build a box-shadow rule, copy the CSS and see it on a sample card. Inset is supported.
tools.lede: Adjust the offset, blur, spread, colour and opacity, watch the shadow on a sample card, then copy the finished declaration.
tools.how: A box shadow takes an optional inset keyword, then the horizontal offset, the vertical offset, the blur radius, the spread radius and a colour, all in that order. Offsets move the shadow away from the element: positive x moves it right and positive y moves it down. The blur radius softens the edge and cannot be negative, while the spread grows the shadow before it is blurred and may be negative to shrink it. The colour field takes a hex value, which is converted to rgba so the opacity field can set the alpha channel separately. The tool rejects values outside these ranges with a specific message, and shows the exact declaration it built.
tools.example: With x 2, y 4, blur 8, spread 0, the colour #000000 and opacity 0.2, the tool produces box-shadow: 2px 4px 8px 0px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.2);. That is a black shadow moved 2 pixels right and 4 pixels down, blurred by 8 pixels, with no spread and 20% opacity, so it reads as a soft grey rather than a black edge.

faq.q: What order do the values go in?
faq.a: Inset first if you want an inner shadow, then the x offset, y offset, blur radius, spread radius and colour. The tool writes them in that order.

faq.q: Why does it refuse a negative blur?
faq.a: A negative blur radius is not valid CSS, so the browser would drop the whole declaration. Offsets and spread may be negative; blur may not.
It grows the shadow shape before the blur is applied. A positive spread makes the shadow larger than the element, a negative spread shrinks it, which is how you get a shadow on one side only.

faq.q: Can I use a colour name instead of hex?
faq.a: This tool takes hex so it can convert it to rgba and apply the opacity slider. With a named colour there is no separate alpha value to adjust.

faq.q: Where do I paste the result?
faq.a: Inside a rule, for example .card { box-shadow: 2px 4px 8px 0px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.2); }. The declaration is exactly what you copy.

tools.keywords: color palette generator tints shades hex rgb swatches
tools.title_tag: Color Palette Generator – Tints and Shades
tools.meta: Enter a hex colour to get five swatches: two tints mixed with white, the base, and two shades mixed with black, with hex and rgb values.
tools.lede: Type a hex colour and the tool mixes it with white and black to give five swatches with both hex and rgb values, ready to copy.
tools.how: Every swatch is a straight mix of the base colour with either white or black, done per channel with the same formula: new channel equals the base channel multiplied by one minus the mix amount, plus the target channel multiplied by the mix amount, rounded to a whole number. Two tints use white at 50% and 25%, the third swatch is the base untouched, and two shades use black at 25% and 50%. Because only the distance to white or black changes, the hue stays in the same family and the swatches step evenly in lightness, which is what a palette needs. Three-digit hex is expanded first, and values outside 0 to 255 cannot occur because the mix is clamped.
tools.example: For #336699 the channels are 51, 102 and 153. The 50% tint gives 51 × 0.5 + 255 × 0.5 = 153, 178.5 and 204, which rounds to #99B3CC. The 25% tint gives #668CB3, the base is #336699, the 25% shade gives #264D73 and the 50% shade gives #1A334D. Each swatch also reports its rgb values, for example rgb(153, 179, 204) for the first tint.

faq.a: Each channel is mixed with 255 at 50% and again at 25%, then rounded. That is a straight linear blend toward white, not a change of hue or saturation.
Two tints, the base and two shades give a usable range of contrast steps without producing colours so close together that they are indistinguishable.

faq.q: Can I paste an rgb() value?
faq.a: Only hex is accepted: three digits such as #06c or six digits such as #336699. Anything else gets a specific error message.
Not necessarily. This tool only mixes colours; check any text and background pair with the contrast checker before using it for text.

faq.q: Does the base colour stay in the list?
faq.a: Yes, it is the middle swatch, unchanged, so you can compare every tint and shade against it.

tools.keywords: password strength checker entropy bits estimate secure
tools.meta: Estimate a password's entropy from its length and the character classes it uses. Runs in the page and is never stored, sent or logged.
tools.lede: Type a password to see how many bits of entropy it represents, which character classes it uses, and how the estimate is calculated.
tools.how: The estimate assumes every character was picked at random from the set the password draws on. That set, the pool, is the sum of the classes in use: 26 for lowercase, 26 for uppercase, 10 for digits, 32 for punctuation and one more for a space. Entropy is the length multiplied by the base-two logarithm of the pool size, which is the same as length × log(pool) ÷ log(2). The bar shows the result against 128 bits and the labels use fixed thresholds printed with the result: under 28 very weak, under 36 weak, under 60 fair, under 80 strong, 80 and above very strong. This is an estimate, not a measurement and not a prediction of how long a guess would take.
tools.example: For Tr0ub4dor&3 the length is 11 and all four classes are present, so the pool is 26 + 26 + 10 + 32 = 94. The base-two logarithm of 94 is 6.5546 bits per character, and 11 × 6.5546 = 72.10 bits, which the tool labels strong because it is between 60 and 80.

faq.a: No. It reports entropy on the assumption that each character was chosen uniformly at random from the pool. A password made of two dictionary words has far less real entropy than its character count suggests.
That is the count of punctuation characters on a standard US keyboard layout. A space adds one more to the pool because it is a separate, usually unexpected character.
They are this tool's fixed bands: under 28 bits very weak, 28 to 35 weak, 36 to 59 fair, 60 to 79 strong, and 80 or more very strong.

faq.q: Is my password sent anywhere or stored?
faq.a: No. It is read in this page, used for the arithmetic and never written to storage, a cookie, the URL or the console. Reloading loses it immediately.

faq.q: Does a long passphrase score well?
faq.a: The figure is an estimate that assumes each character is picked at random. A phrase built from real words is far weaker than its length suggests, because the words come from a small dictionary an attacker can try first. For reference, 20 characters drawn at random from 26 lowercase letters would give 20 × log₂(26) = 94.01 bits; a 20-character sentence of ordinary words does not.

ui.empty: Type a password to see the estimate.
ui.tooLong: That password is longer than {max} characters. The estimate does not need more than that.
ui.noChars: That input contains no characters this tool can classify.
ui.note: Estimated in your browser: the password is never stored, logged or sent anywhere.

tools.keywords: favicon generator png sizes icon apple touch android pwa
tools.title_tag: Favicon Generator – PNG Sizes From One Image
tools.meta: Turn one image into favicon PNGs at 16, 32, 48, 180, 192 and 512 pixels, drawn on a canvas in your browser. Nothing is uploaded.
tools.lede: Choose an image and the tool draws it into six square PNG files, with a download button for each size and a progress bar as it works.
tools.how: The image is decoded by the browser first, and an image that fails to decode is reported instead of producing blank files. Favicons must be square, so the largest centred square of your image is used and the rest is cropped away. That square is then drawn into a canvas at each size in the list, using the canvas smoothing settings, and each canvas is exported as a PNG blob. Every size gets its own download button, and the file size of each PNG is shown next to it. Uploads are capped at 5 MB and empty files are rejected, because an empty file cannot be decoded. The image never leaves the page: the canvas work happens in your browser.
tools.example: Upload a 1024 by 1024 PNG and the tool produces six files: 16, 32, 48, 180, 192 and 512 pixels square. Because the source is already square there is no crop, and the 512 file is exactly 512 by 512 pixels. A 1000 by 800 image would first be cropped to the centre 800 by 800 square, then scaled down to those same six sizes.

faq.a: 16 and 32 for browser tabs, 48 for Windows shortcuts, 180 for the Apple touch icon, 192 for Android home screens and 512 for stores and web app manifests. The page produces all six.
A favicon has to be square, so the largest centred square is taken and the edges are dropped. Nothing is stretched, which would distort the artwork.
No. It is read into an image element and drawn on a canvas inside the page. There is no network request and no storage.
Any format the browser can decode, which usually means PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF and SVG. The output is always PNG regardless of the input.
No. It writes PNG files, which browsers and web app manifests accept for these sizes. An .ico is a separate container format and is not produced here.

ui.cap: Images up to 5 MB. The file is read in this tab and never uploaded.
ui.emptyFile: That file is empty, so there is nothing to draw. Choose an image with content.
ui.tooBig: That file is larger than {max}. Use a smaller image.
ui.notImage: That is not an image file. Choose a PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF or SVG.
ui.done: Finished. Download the sizes you need.
ui.badImage: That file could not be read as an image. It may be damaged or not really an image.
